clue.text: Swashbuckler chap regularly ordered a pint with claret chaser

indicators.note: something done regularly happens at even intervals, so every other letter of the word is kept
to order things is to arrange them afresh, so these letters are put into a new sequence

blocks.note: the first and third letters of the word
taken as written, ready to be rearranged
claret is old boxing slang for blood

explanation.surface: A dashing pirate type orders a pint with a glass of red wine to follow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chaser' is a drink taken after another, so BLOOD comes last. Claret, the red Bordeaux wine, is also slang for blood, as in a bloody nose.
explanation.definitionFit: Captain Blood is the swashbuckling pirate hero of Sabatini's novel and the Errol Flynn film, an example of the genre.

clue.text: Cheese sandwich made for Ms Gabler by His Majesty

indicators.note: a sandwich has bread on both sides of a filling, so one piece encloses the other

blocks.note: Carolus Rex, King Charles's royal cipher
Hedda Gabler is the title heroine of Ibsen's play

explanation.surface: The King makes a cheese sandwich for a woman called Gabler.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface sandwich is a lunch; really the royal cipher is the bread around the Ibsen heroine. Carolus Rex is Latin for King Charles.
explanation.definitionFit: Cheddar is a hard English cheese named after a Somerset village, so it is an example of the category.

clue.text: Place on tee and hit golf ball

blocks.note: to place something is to put it
tee is the spoken name of the letter T

explanation.surface: A golfer sets the ball on a tee and strikes it.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'on' puts one piece above the other, so the letter follows the verb. The tee is the golf peg, but here it is just the letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A putt is the gentle stroke on the green that rolls the golf ball towards the hole.

clue.text: Leave crab and onion wraps

indicators.note: a wrap encloses its contents, so the run of words holds the solution inside them

blocks.note: the letters run across the three words, after the first two

explanation.surface: Someone is told to skip the crab and onion wraps on a menu.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wraps' reads as a food item, the tortilla rolls on the menu, but it is the verb telling you the solution is held within.
explanation.definitionFit: To abandon a place, person or plan is to leave it behind for good; the two verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: Hamstrung knight walked awkwardly out of hospital

indicators.note: going out of something means leaving it, so a letter departs from the word

blocks.note: N is the chess notation for a knight
to hobble is to walk with difficulty
H is the abbreviation for hospital, as on road signs

explanation.surface: An injured knight limps away from hospital.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures a discharged patient; really the letter for hospital leaves the limping word, and the knight's letter goes in front.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words mean deliberately disabled or hindered; nobbling is tampering with a racehorse or a rival to stop it competing.

clue.text: Early riser first to launch disaster recovery vessel

indicators.note: the first of a word is its opening letter, so only that one is kept

blocks.note: the opening letter of the word
Noah's ark carried survivors through the Flood

explanation.surface: Someone up early is first to launch a rescue boat after a disaster.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Launch' tempts as a boat; it only supplies its first letter. The Flood is the disaster the ark rode out.
explanation.definitionFit: The skylark sings at dawn, so a lark is the usual word for a person who gets up early.

clue.text: Dark Quarter periodically holding up Oxford's no. 1 science grad

indicators.note: something happening periodically recurs at intervals, so alternate letters are kept
number one is the first, so only the opening letter is kept

blocks.note: the opening letter of the city's name
BSc, Bachelor of Science, a science graduate's degree
the second, fourth and sixth letters

explanation.surface: A gloomy district of town delays an Oxford science graduate.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'holding up' means supporting from below, so the alternate letters sit underneath the graduate's pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Obscure in its literal sense means gloomy or poorly lit, a synonym for dark.

clue.text: Classes left boozer last of all and discovered nice community

indicators.note: the last of a word is its closing letter, so only that one is kept
dis-covered means with the covering taken off, so the outer letters go and the inside stays

blocks.note: genera are biological classes, plural of genus
L is the abbreviation for left
a boozer is British slang for a pub
the closing letter of the word
the word with its first and last letters stripped

explanation.surface: Students leave the pub at closing time and find a pleasant neighbourhood.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Discovered' reads as found, but it means uncovered, the outer letters removed. 'Boozer' is British slang for a pub.
explanation.definitionFit: The general public is ordinary people as a whole, the community at large rather than any special group.

clue.text: Awful traffic northbound – roadster is written off in serious incident

indicators.note: a down entry is read top to bottom, so travelling north runs it the other way
a written-off car is a wreck, so these letters are smashed up and rebuilt

blocks.note: a traffic jam, the awful sort of traffic
taken as written, ready to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Northbound traffic is terrible after a sports car is wrecked in a crash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Northbound' sounds like a traffic report but is the reversal signal in a down clue; 'written off' describes the car and also the letter shake-up.
explanation.definitionFit: A major disaster is a grave event or catastrophe, the same idea as a serious incident.

clue.text: Laid back upstart celebrity entertaining complex character

indicators.note: something laid back is set down the wrong way, so the letters run right to left
to entertain guests is to have them inside, so the words hold the letters within

blocks.note: the letters straddling the two words, from the end of one into the start of the other

explanation.surface: A relaxed new celebrity plays host to a tricky personality.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Laid back' reads as relaxed and describes the upstart, but it tells you to read the run of letters backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Electra lends her name to the Electra complex in psychology, so she is literally a character behind a complex.

clue.text: One for whom work is a daily grind, though there are perks?

definitions.text: One for whom work is a daily grind, though there are perks?

blocks.clueFragment: One for whom work is a daily grind, though there are perks?
blocks.note: surface reading: a worker in a dull, repetitive job that has some fringe benefits
setter's reading: someone who literally grinds coffee beans every day
setter's reading: coffee perks, short for percolates

explanation.walkthrough: 'Daily grind' and 'perks' are office clichés about a dreary job, but both are coffee words: beans are ground, and coffee perks in a percolator.
explanation.definitionFit: A barista makes espresso drinks in a coffee bar, grinding beans and brewing all day long.

clue.text: Roosevelt wasting time in whirlpool

indicators.note: to waste something is to lose it, so a letter is thrown away

blocks.note: Teddy was the nickname of President Theodore Roosevelt
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: A US president fritters away time in a swirling pool.
explanation.walkthrough: Theodore Roosevelt's nickname, which gave us the teddy bear, loses its opening letter for time.
explanation.definitionFit: An eddy is a small circular current of water, a miniature version of a whirlpool.

clue.text: Blue diamonds in unopened crypt

indicators.note: with no opening means without its first letter, which is the way in
being in something means sitting inside it, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: D is the card-game abbreviation for diamonds
a vault is an underground burial chamber

explanation.surface: Blue gems lie in a sealed tomb.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blue' looks like the colour of the diamonds, but it is the definition in its risqué sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Blue and adult both describe explicit, sexually frank material, as in a blue film or adult content.

clue.text: Victor Hotel Uniform: you are cleared for take-off

blocks.note: Hotel is H in the NATO phonetic alphabet
Uniform is U in the NATO phonetic alphabet
the signal that permission has been given to start

explanation.surface: An air traffic controller spells out a call sign and gives clearance to take off.
explanation.walkthrough: All three call-sign words seem to be phonetic letters, but Victor is the definition rather than a V. The other two give their initials.
explanation.definitionFit: The definition names a first name: the French novelist Victor Hugo, author of Les Misérables, completes it.

clue.text: Riddle is put up the night before

indicators.note: in a down clue lifting something up turns it to read bottom to top

blocks.note: taken as written
the eve is the evening or day before an event

explanation.surface: A puzzle is posted the evening before.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Riddle' looks like a puzzle, but it is the noun for a coarse garden sieve, as in riddling soil.
explanation.definitionFit: A riddle is a large coarse-meshed sieve for separating soil or gravel, so the two are synonyms.

clue.text: It's often presented in March, or it comes after November

blocks.note: first meaning: the Academy Award statuette, handed out at the spring ceremony
second meaning: the code word following N in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.walkthrough: The months make it look like a calendar clue, but November is a call sign, and the next one in the phonetic alphabet answers it.
explanation.definitionFit: The Academy Awards statuette has the nickname, and the phonetic alphabet uses the same name for the letter O.

clue.text: Put on trial after unwrapping margarine spread

indicators.note: taking the wrapper off removes the outside, so the first and last letters go
spreading something moves it about, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written before its outer letters go

explanation.surface: Someone is taken to court after opening a tub of margarine and spreading it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spread' is what you do with margarine, but here it is the verb shuffling the stripped letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To arraign someone is to call them before a court to answer a criminal charge, formally putting them on trial.

clue.text: "Stretch out, lay back, Sid" – nurse

indicators.note: lying back tips something the other way round, so the letters read right to left

blocks.note: taken as written
to nurse someone is to tend them

explanation.surface: A nurse tells a patient called Sid to stretch out and lie back.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation looks like a nurse's instruction; really 'nurse' is a verb giving the second piece.
explanation.definitionFit: To distend is to swell or stretch out from internal pressure, as a stomach does.

clue.text: China State conference that's boring

blocks.note: china plate is Cockney rhyming slang for mate
to aver is to state firmly

explanation.surface: A Chinese government meeting is dull.
explanation.walkthrough: China and State read as the country and its government; really china is rhyming slang (china plate, mate) and State is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A palaver is a long, tedious discussion; the word began as a parley or negotiation between traders and locals.

clue.text: More eminent old newspaper that is accepted by both sides

indicators.note: something accepted is taken in, so those pieces go inside the others

blocks.note: L and R, left and right
O is the abbreviation for old
the FT is the Financial Times
i.e., Latin id est, means that is

explanation.surface: A respected old newspaper's line is accepted across the political spectrum.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Both sides' sounds political but means the two side letters, left and right, which enclose the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: Lofty means of high rank or exalted, so the comparative form matches a more eminent person.

clue.text: Consider again murder inquiry at Cluedo?

blocks.note: the Reverend Green, one of the suspects in the murder board game Cluedo
the question a player asks while guessing the killer

explanation.surface: A detective reopens a murder case set in a board game.
explanation.walkthrough: The question a Cluedo player might put is whether the Reverend is the culprit: Rev, is it? The question mark flags the playful parse.
explanation.definitionFit: To revisit an issue is to come back to it and think it over once more.

clue.text: Lettuce stuffed with seaweed? It stinks!

indicators.note: a stuffed thing has filling put inside it, so one piece encloses another

blocks.note: cos is a variety of lettuce, also called romaine
an alga is a simple water plant such as seaweed

explanation.surface: Someone recoils from lettuce filled with seaweed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It stinks!' sounds like a verdict on the salad but is the definition, describing the smelly fuel gas.
explanation.definitionFit: Coal gas, once piped to homes for lighting and cooking, has a strong unpleasant smell, so a cryptic hint describes it.

clue.text: Discuss the latest game failing to kick off in knockout trophy

indicators.note: not starting means losing the beginning, so the first letter goes
being in something means sitting inside it, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: a cup is the trophy for a knockout competition
a match is a game

explanation.surface: Fans chat about the latest cup tie, which failed to start.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kick off' sounds footballing but just means the start of the word goes.
explanation.definitionFit: To catch up with friends is to chat about recent news, swapping the latest happenings.

clue.text: Head of Government permits instrument of execution

indicators.note: the head of a word is its opening letter, so only that one is kept

blocks.note: the opening letter of the word
to permit is to allow

explanation.surface: The prime minister authorises a method of execution.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Head of Government' reads as a leader, but only the first letter is wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: The gallows is the wooden frame from which people were hanged, a device for carrying out executions.

clue.text: Lifelong buddy pens no. 1 hit

indicators.note: to pen something is to shut it in an enclosure, so one piece holds another

blocks.note: BFF is texting shorthand for best friend forever
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: An old friend writes a chart-topping song.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pens' suggests writing a hit record, but it means enclosing, and 'hit' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Biff is informal for a punch or blow, so as a verb it means to hit someone.

clue.text: Musical case missing front cover is returned

indicators.note: a book missing its front cover has lost what comes first, so the opening letter goes
something returned comes back the way it went, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: the dative is a grammatical case

explanation.surface: A music case with its front cover gone is sent back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Case' looks like a container for sheet music, but it is grammatical: the dative is the case of the indirect object in Latin and German.
explanation.definitionFit: Evita is the Lloyd Webber and Rice stage musical about Eva Perón, an example of the genre.

clue.text: Nom de plume one shunned, sadly

indicators.note: something shunned is avoided and kept out, so a letter is dropped

blocks.note: a pen name is an alias
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A writer's pen name was regrettably avoided.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove the Roman one from the assumed name; 'sadly' is the definition, not a comment on the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Alas is an interjection expressing regret, used where we might say unfortunately or sadly.

clue.text: Very embarrassed after knocking over diesel oil

indicators.note: knocking something over upends it, so in a down clue the letters turn bottom to top

blocks.note: V is the abbreviation for very
red in the face from embarrassment

explanation.surface: Someone is mortified after spilling diesel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' puts the colour behind the abbreviation; the whole lot is then turned over. Derv is the British name for diesel fuel for road vehicles.
explanation.definitionFit: Derv comes from diesel-engined road vehicle and is the British trade term for that fuel, so it is a synonym.

clue.text: Returning, delivers music box

indicators.note: something returning comes back the way it went, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: a rapper raps, delivering lyrics rhythmically over music

explanation.surface: A courier comes back with a music box.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Music box' looks like one object, but the break falls between them, and 'box' is the verb for fighting.
explanation.definitionFit: To spar is to box for practice, trading punches with a training partner.

clue.text: Froideur is since dissipated

indicators.note: something dissipated is scattered, so these letters are dispersed and reassembled

blocks.note: taken as written, ready to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A cool atmosphere between people has since cleared.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Froideur' is the French-derived word for coolness in manner, used in English for an unfriendly atmosphere.
explanation.definitionFit: Froideur is coldness or aloofness between people, and iciness is the same frosty unfriendliness.

clue.text: Stick up for the brewing industry with hard work by European

definitions.text: Stick up for the brewing industry

blocks.note: H is the pencil abbreviation for hard
op is short for opus, a work
a Pole is a person from Poland

explanation.surface: A hardworking European defends the beer industry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stick up for' reads as a phrasal verb meaning defend; really it is a stick that stands up, supporting a crop used by brewers.
explanation.definitionFit: A hop-pole is the tall upright stake on which hop vines are trained, and hops flavour beer.

clue.text: Gutted, poor poor 24 Across divides sensitive regions

indicators.note: a gutted fish has its insides taken out, so only the outer letters remain
something in poor shape is in a bad state, so these letters are knocked into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written before its insides go
the answer to that clue, ready to be rearranged
to divide something is to part it

explanation.surface: Splitting up sensitive areas leaves the poor feeling gutted.
explanation.walkthrough: The repeated 'poor' does two jobs: the first gives letters, emptied of its middle; the second shuffles the musical.
explanation.definitionFit: Private parts is a euphemism for the genitals, the most sensitive and intimate regions of the body.
